rv.q: "Wonderfully crafted…Poignancy mixes well with humor, the songs are fresh and sweet, the set is blissful and the performances honest. It has a polished feel. All of the parts work smartly….
“Tuck Everlasting,” a warm-spirited and piercingly touching musical that has nothing flashy or splashy about it.
I feel the same about the future of this enchanting long-shot of a show.

This adaptation of Natalie Babbitt's beloved children's novel about a family cursed with eternal life has been turned into a gentle, old-fashioned musical that's heavy on sentiment and light on surprises.
Those who lean that way will be attracted to the tuneful folk-meets-Broadway score, to the solid performances and to the gentle Americana fable.
But it removes much of the tension from a story filled with agonizing decision-making and enough talk of life and death to keep anyone awake at night.
Charmingly illustrating the stages of a long life marked by love and loss, it achieves a level of subtle artistry that makes everything preceding it seem pedestrian by comparison.

Still, “Tuck Everlasting” realizes enough of its ambitions to be watchable, and Casey Nicholaw’s staging is full of quiet delights, though his swirly choreography, especially in the show’s climactic ballet, is bland.
But the show’s spirit is ultimately touching
For all Tuck’s thematic concerns with immortality, I doubt a long life awaits it in this competitive market for Broadway family fare.
It’s pretty crazy that this story about regret, mortality and big life choices — make that “eternal life or death” choices — could end up so toothless.
I found it to be a musical for the child in someone else.

All of which is my circuitous way of avoiding the mostly depressing task of writing about the latest Tuck family visit, in the form of a Broadway musical so treacly you may leave the Broadhurst Theatre wanting to kick a puppy.
A polite misfire of a musical about immortality that feels like it goes on forever.
Tuck Everlasting is a real heart-tugger.
Lovely, honest, and ultimately moving, in the ways that matter most, it's what a musical should be.
The folksy score (by composer Chris Miller and lyricist Nathan Tysen) emphasizes a child’s sense of wonder, along with some tender spots.
This interpretation of “Tuck Everlasting” is neither tragic nor cynical.
The result is endearing family entertainment.

An ineffectual, slow-paced Act 1 is followed by a solid and compelling Act 2 and a charming, emotionally-moving sustained dance sequence that concludes the musical. It’s a shame that the whole show isn’t as good as the second half. Tuck Everlasting is still a fine work of art for its family show genre.
Characters are pretty sketchy, but the cast makes the most of what they’ve got.
Considering its theme, however, it could have been much more.
Director-choreographer Casey Nicholaw’s staggering finale is the only scene that completely fulfills Tuck Everlasting’s obvious aim to be one of those musicals that appeal to children of all ages.
Once again, this singular artist takes a gamble that pays big dividends.
Much like the current revival of The Color Purple, I have a feeling that in a decade or so, we may see a very different reimagining of Tuck Everlasting—one that is older and perhaps a bit wiser.
There's one salient takeaway from Tuck Everlasting, the lackluster new Broadway musical based on Natalie Babbitt's beloved 1975 children's novel
Wholesome, moral winsomeness will never go out of style, presumably; but a rousing musical it does not make, at least in the case of Tuck Everlasting.
Everything from the costuming to the set to the choreography to the direction plays loud, harsh, and cartoonish doing a disservice to the sincere characters and fine work of the actors.
More than anything else in “Tuck Everlasting,” their lax narrative gives us a real glimpse of just how long forever can be.
Tuck Everlasting will tug at your heartstrings and bring you to your feet at the end.
I will say, hopefully without bias, that I just loved this musical.
As a lovely tale about the joys and dangers that come with being alive, “Tuck Everlasting” makes for a very refreshing experience.
Fortunately, this period production fares much better in the stage translation.
A beautiful set, expert choreography and memorable score aid and brilliant acting aid the storytelling, and it all adds to the play’s fantasy theme.
Tuck Everlasting is an imaginative and faithful adaptation of Natalie Babbitt's timeless children's novel that successfully leaves the audience pondering: if you could live forever, would you?
It's one of the relatively few takeaways from a show that, despite running about two and a quarter hours, sometimes feels as though it should be called Tuck Neverending.
It’s in its last 15 minutes or so that Tuck Everlasting shakes off its quotidian nature.
Both these shows should never have come to Broadway but if the producers just want to lose money so be it.
Tuck Everlasting is a well-intentioned musical but ultimately presents nothing new.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics find this family-friendly musical earnest and touching but modest, with a beautiful finale that elevates an otherwise uneven show. The sincere storytelling resonates, yet lacks the theatrical magic to compete with flashier Broadway fare.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
